Rice|||Rice blast: Grow a rice variety with resistance to blast that is recommended for your region.
Use healthy, certified seed and follow the local seed-treatment recommendation where blast is a recurring problem.
Avoid excessive nitrogen; apply nitrogen in balanced, split doses rather than one heavy application.
Monitor leaves and necks regularly, remove volunteer rice and infected crop residues, and avoid moisture stress during susceptible growth stages.
Rice|||Brown spot: Use healthy, certified seed and a variety with good brown-spot tolerance where available.
Correct soil-fertility problems using a soil test; maintain balanced nitrogen and adequate potassium and other nutrients.
Remove or incorporate infected rice residues and rotate with a suitable non-host crop where practical.
Maintain a healthy crop with reliable water management; avoid prolonged nutrient or moisture stress.
Rice|||Bacterial leaf blight: Plant resistant or tolerant rice varieties recommended for the local area.
Avoid clipping seedling leaf tips during transplanting, because wounds can help the bacterium enter.
Use balanced nitrogen and avoid excessive nitrogen top-dressing.
Keep fields and bunds free of volunteer rice and grassy hosts; avoid moving through or handling plants when foliage is wet.
Rice|||Sheath blight: Use wider, locally recommended plant spacing and avoid an excessively dense canopy.
Avoid excessive nitrogen; apply fertilizer in balanced split doses.
Remove or incorporate infected crop residues and manage grasses/weeds that can harbour the pathogen.
Inspect lower leaf sheaths regularly and seek local plant-pathology advice if lesions begin spreading.
Rice|||False smut: Choose varieties with better tolerance to false smut where locally available.
Use healthy seed and avoid excessive nitrogen, particularly late heavy applications.
Scout panicles around flowering and remove infected smut balls carefully before they rupture and release spores.
Manage infected crop residues after harvest and follow local advisories for any flowering-stage treatment.
Wheat|||Wheat stem rust: Grow rust-resistant wheat varieties recommended for your production zone.
Inspect stems and leaf sheaths regularly, especially as the crop approaches heading and grain filling.
Remove volunteer wheat plants and avoid carrying infected plant material between fields.
Use a locally registered rust fungicide only when disease risk and extension advisories justify it; follow the label.
Wheat|||Wheat leaf rust: Choose a leaf-rust-resistant variety suited to your region and sow within the recommended window.
Monitor the lower and middle leaves frequently for new orange-brown pustules.
Remove volunteer wheat and manage crop residues that can maintain the green bridge between seasons.
Where disease is increasing, use a locally approved fungicide only on the advice of an agricultural extension service and follow its label.
Wheat|||Loose smut: Use certified, loose-smut-free seed from a reliable source.
Treat seed with a locally registered systemic seed treatment specifically recommended for loose smut; follow the product label.
Rogue and remove smutted heads before the black spore masses disperse over healthy flowers.
Grow resistant or less-susceptible varieties where available and avoid saving seed from affected fields.
Maize|||Turcicum leaf blight: Plant resistant or tolerant maize hybrids recommended for your area.
Rotate with a non-host crop and manage infected maize residues after harvest to reduce carry-over inoculum.
Maintain recommended plant spacing and balanced fertilization to avoid a dense, stressed canopy.
Scout lower leaves regularly; use a locally approved foliar fungicide only when disease severity and local advice warrant it.
Maize|||Maydis leaf blight: Select maize hybrids with resistance or tolerance to maydis leaf blight.
Rotate away from maize and remove or properly incorporate infected maize residues.
Use recommended plant spacing and avoid excessive nitrogen that produces a dense canopy.
Monitor lesions during humid weather and follow local extension guidance before applying any registered fungicide.
Maize|||Common rust: Grow maize hybrids with good common-rust resistance for the local region.
Scout leaves regularly, particularly during cool, humid weather and before tasseling.
Remove volunteer maize plants and manage crop residues between seasons where practical.
If rust becomes severe on a susceptible hybrid, use a locally registered fungicide only according to extension advice and label directions.
Maize|||Bacterial stalk rot: Improve field drainage and avoid prolonged waterlogging around the root zone.
Avoid mechanical injury to stalks and roots during cultivation and field operations.
Use balanced nitrogen and potassium fertilization; avoid excessive nitrogen.
Remove and destroy severely rotted plants after diagnosis, clean equipment, and rotate with a non-host crop.
Tomato|||Early blight: Remove and dispose of infected lower leaves and crop debris; do not leave diseased residue beside the plants.
Rotate tomato with non-solanaceous crops for at least 2–3 seasons where feasible.
Use clean seed or seedlings, mulch the soil to reduce splash, and avoid overhead irrigation.
Stake plants and maintain recommended spacing for airflow; use a locally approved fungicide only if disease pressure warrants it.
Tomato|||Late blight: Use healthy transplants and, where available, late-blight-resistant tomato varieties.
Remove and destroy infected plants and nearby volunteer potato/tomato plants or cull piles that can maintain the pathogen.
Improve drainage and airflow; irrigate at the soil level and avoid prolonged leaf wetness.
During cool, wet, high-risk weather, follow local late-blight alerts and use only a locally registered fungicide according to its label.
Tomato|||Bacterial wilt: Remove wilted plants with as much of the root system as possible and dispose of them safely; do not compost diseased plants.
Use disease-free seedlings and resistant/tolerant varieties or grafted plants where suitable.
Rotate with non-host crops such as cereals; rotation alone may not eliminate the long-lived soil pathogen.
Improve drainage and sanitize tools, trays and footwear; avoid moving infested soil or irrigation water to clean plots.
Tomato|||Tomato yellow leaf curl disease: Use resistant or tolerant tomato varieties where available and start with healthy, virus-free seedlings.
Remove and safely destroy symptomatic plants early to reduce virus sources in the field.
Protect nurseries with insect-proof netting and use reflective mulch or physical barriers to reduce whitefly landings.
Remove weeds and volunteer host plants; monitor whiteflies and use integrated vector management. Insecticides may not prevent virus transmission.
Potato|||Common scab: Plant certified, healthy seed tubers and choose a less-susceptible variety where available.
Keep soil moisture steady during tuber initiation and early development; avoid dry soil during this period.
Avoid liming or adding alkaline materials immediately before potato planting; adjust soil pH only on the basis of a soil test and local advice.
Rotate with non-host crops and avoid repeatedly planting potato in the same scab-affected field.
Potato|||Black scurf: Use certified seed tubers with minimal black scurf and discard badly affected tubers.
Use a locally registered seed-tuber treatment or recommended biological treatment where advised.
Rotate with non-host crops and manage volunteer potatoes and infected crop residues.
Plant into well-prepared soil at the recommended time and harvest when tuber skins have matured to reduce injury and infection.
Potato|||Potato late blight: Plant certified disease-free seed tubers and choose resistant or tolerant varieties when available.
Destroy volunteer potato plants and cull piles, and remove infected foliage promptly where practical.
Earth up adequately to protect developing tubers and improve field drainage; avoid overhead irrigation and prolonged leaf wetness.
Monitor local late-blight warnings and use only locally registered fungicides according to the label and resistance-management advice.
Chilli|||Anthracnose / fruit rot: Use disease-free seed and healthy transplants; use a recommended seed treatment where locally advised.
Remove and destroy infected fruits regularly, including fallen fruits, to reduce spore production.
Rotate with non-host crops and avoid planting chilli continuously in the same field.
Maintain plant spacing and drainage, avoid overhead irrigation, and use a locally approved fungicide only when recommended.
Chilli|||Bacterial leaf spot: Start with pathogen-free seed and healthy transplants; avoid seed saved from affected plants.
Remove infected plant debris and rotate with non-host crops for 2–3 seasons where practical.
Avoid working in the crop while leaves are wet and use drip or soil-level irrigation instead of overhead watering.
Disinfect tools and trays; use copper-based or other bactericide products only if registered locally and recommended by an extension specialist.
Brinjal|||Phomopsis blight and fruit rot: Use healthy seed from disease-free fruits and follow a locally recommended seed-treatment protocol.
Collect and destroy infected fruits, leaves and stems; do not leave diseased material in the field.
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops for 2–3 seasons and remove volunteer brinjal plants.
Maintain adequate spacing, drainage and airflow, and avoid overhead irrigation that keeps foliage and fruits wet.
Brinjal|||Bacterial wilt: Remove and safely destroy wilted plants with their roots; do not replant immediately into the same planting hole.
Use healthy seedlings and tolerant varieties or grafted plants where locally available.
Rotate with non-host crops, especially cereals or other crops advised for the field's pathogen history.
Improve drainage and sanitize tools, trays and footwear; avoid transferring soil or water from affected areas.
Cabbage|||Black rot: Use certified disease-free seed and healthy transplants; use a validated hot-water seed treatment only under local extension guidance.
Grow resistant or tolerant cabbage varieties where available.
Rotate with non-cruciferous crops for at least 2–3 seasons and destroy infected cabbage residues and cruciferous weeds.
Avoid handling plants when wet, and use clean nursery trays, tools and irrigation water to limit bacterial spread.
Cabbage|||Clubroot: Use resistant or tolerant varieties where available and start with clean, disease-free transplants.
Test soil and apply agricultural lime only as recommended to adjust acidic soil; the target pH depends on local soil conditions.
Use a long rotation away from cruciferous crops (often 7 years or longer in heavily infested fields) because resting spores persist in soil.
Prevent movement of contaminated soil: clean tools, footwear and machinery, and improve drainage in affected plots.
Groundnut|||Tikka leaf spot (early and l: Grow varieties with improved resistance or tolerance to early and late leaf spots.
Rotate groundnut with cereals and remove or incorporate infected groundnut residues after harvest.
Maintain recommended spacing and control weeds to improve airflow and reduce prolonged leaf wetness.
Inspect lower leaves regularly and follow local extension advice for a registered fungicide if disease begins to increase.
Groundnut|||Groundnut rust: Choose groundnut varieties with good rust tolerance where available.
Inspect the lower leaf surfaces regularly for early rust pustules, especially in humid weather.
Rotate crops and manage volunteer groundnut plants and infected residues between seasons.
Use a locally registered rust fungicide only when disease pressure warrants it; follow label directions and local spray advisories.
Sugarcane|||Red rot: Plant healthy, disease-free seed cane setts from inspected fields and use varieties resistant to locally prevalent red-rot strains.
Rogue and destroy infected clumps and do not use setts from diseased canes for planting.
Disinfect cutting tools and avoid moving infected cane trash or setts between fields.
Follow locally recommended sett treatment and crop rotation practices; maintain field sanitation and good drainage.
Sugarcane|||Smut: Use resistant sugarcane varieties recommended for the area and plant healthy, disease-free setts.
Inspect fields regularly and remove smut-whip-bearing clumps before the whip releases spores; bag the whip before removal.
Destroy infected clumps and avoid using setts from affected stools.
Apply a locally approved sett-treatment protocol and clean cutting tools and transport equipment between fields.
Banana|||Panama disease (Fusarium wilt): Plant certified disease-free tissue-culture plants or healthy planting material from a verified clean source.
Do not move suckers, soil, water, tools or machinery from infested areas into clean fields; disinfect equipment and footwear.
Remove and destroy infected mats according to local agricultural or quarantine guidance; do not use their suckers for propagation.
Use resistant or tolerant cultivars suitable for the local Fusarium variant and avoid replanting susceptible banana in heavily infested soil.
Banana|||Black Sigatoka: Remove heavily infected and dead leaves, or trim infected portions, to reduce the amount of disease-producing tissue.
Maintain recommended spacing, drainage and canopy ventilation so leaves dry more quickly.
Remove or manage infected leaf debris and monitor new leaves regularly for disease progression.
Where needed, use only locally registered fungicides under an extension spray advisory and rotate modes of action to slow resistance.
Mango|||Anthracnose: Prune dead and diseased twigs and open the canopy to improve air circulation and reduce leaf wetness.
Collect and dispose of fallen, rotting and mummified fruits and infected panicles.
Avoid overhead irrigation during flowering and fruit development; maintain good orchard sanitation.
Use only locally recommended pre-harvest or post-harvest disease-management treatments, and keep harvest crates and storage areas clean.
Mango|||Powdery mildew: Prune crowded branches and maintain an open canopy so panicles dry quickly.
Monitor new panicles and flowers closely, especially during cool or humid flowering weather.
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization, which can encourage dense, susceptible growth.
Remove badly affected panicles where practical and use a locally registered mildew treatment only at the recommended crop stage.
Citrus|||Citrus canker: Use certified disease-free nursery plants and avoid bringing infected citrus material into the orchard.
Prune and destroy infected twigs when foliage is dry, following local plant-health or quarantine guidance.
Disinfect pruning tools and avoid working among wet plants, which can spread bacteria.
Establish windbreaks where suitable and manage citrus leafminer through integrated pest management to reduce entry wounds.
Papaya|||Papaya ringspot disease: Use healthy, virus-free seedlings and plant resistant or tolerant varieties where available.
Rogue and safely remove infected papaya plants as soon as symptoms are recognised; there is no curative treatment for an infected plant.
Remove nearby volunteer papaya and weed hosts that may maintain the virus between crops.
Use physical protection for young plants and plan new plantings away from infected papaya blocks; aphid insecticides alone may not stop rapid virus transmission.
Grapevine|||Downy mildew: Train vines and manage the canopy with suitable shoot positioning and leaf removal so foliage dries quickly.
Improve drainage and avoid overhead irrigation or other practices that keep leaves wet overnight.
Remove infected leaves and shoots and manage vineyard floor debris to reduce local inoculum.
Monitor weather and disease alerts; use locally registered downy-mildew products only as advised and rotate modes of action.
Onion|||Purple blotch: Use healthy seed or sets and follow a locally recommended seed treatment when necessary.
Rotate onion with non-allium crops and remove or incorporate infected crop residues.
Use recommended spacing and drip irrigation to reduce leaf wetness; avoid late-day overhead irrigation.
Maintain balanced nutrition, particularly avoiding excessive nitrogen, and follow local fungicide advice if lesions spread.
Okra|||Yellow vein mosaic disease: Plant resistant or tolerant okra varieties recommended for the region.
Remove and destroy infected plants early to reduce sources of the virus.
Protect nursery seedlings with insect-proof netting and monitor whiteflies using yellow sticky traps.
Remove weeds and volunteer host plants around the field and use integrated whitefly management; do not rely on insecticides alone to cure infected plants.
Soybean|||Soybean rust: Use locally adapted varieties with improved rust resistance or tolerance where available.
Scout the lower canopy frequently and follow regional disease alerts during humid periods.
Destroy volunteer soybean plants and manage infected crop residues between seasons.
If rust is confirmed and increasing, use a locally registered fungicide at the advised stage and rotate modes of action according to the label.
Cotton|||Bacterial blight: Plant certified, disease-free seed and choose varieties with resistance to bacterial blight.
Remove or destroy infected crop residues after harvest and manage volunteer cotton plants.
Rotate with non-host crops and avoid moving through the field when plants are wet.
Maintain recommended spacing and drainage; use seed treatment or bactericide measures only when included in local extension guidance.
Peanut|||Stem rot (southern blight): Rotate peanut with cereals such as maize or sorghum and avoid continuous peanut cultivation in the same field.
Improve drainage and avoid excessive irrigation, especially around the plant crown.
Remove and destroy wilted plants with nearby infected debris and soil as appropriate; clean tools before moving between fields.
Use well-decomposed organic amendments or locally validated biocontrol agents such as Trichoderma where recommended; use fungicides only under local extension guidance.
